method: Each quote was matched verbatim (case/curly-quote/whitespace-normalized) against the fetched source page text. Unverified quotes were dropped. Profiles added 12 Oct 2026 (Dolmayan onward): the same rule. Each quote was matched word for word against the fetched page; some pages are reposts on fan archives, which the caption says. Quotes that could not be fetched and matched were dropped.

signature_techniques.claim: Long, intricate passages in odd time signatures, and a wide range of percussion beyond the kit: orchestra bells, tubular bells, wind chimes, crotales, timbales, timpani, gong, temple blocks.
Added Simmons electronic drums and Akai samplers starting with Grace Under Pressure (1984).

gear.claim: Played Slingerland, Tama, Ludwig and Drum Workshop (DW) drums with Rush, in that order.
Zildjian A-series cymbals and Wuhan chinas until the early 2000s, then Sabian's Paragon line, made for him (launched 2004).
A rotating drum riser: acoustic kit in front, electronic kit behind.

feel.claim: After 20 years spent on time, tempo and 'shadings of rhythmic feel', he said confidence was the key to his playing (MD 1989).
Began studying with Freddie Gruber in 1994 and reworked his style with jazz and swing elements; later studied with Peter Erskine.
In 2011 he described himself as moving from a 'compositional' drummer toward an improvisational one.

influences.claim: Early on: Keith Moon, Ginger Baker, John Bonham. Later: Gene Krupa and Buddy Rich. Also cites Billy Cobham and Bill Bruford.

arranging.claim: Rush's primary lyricist as well as its drummer.
Said writing and arranging songs, including working out drum patterns, was 'the center of everything' for him. By 1989 he could hear a demo with 'a wide open mind'.

impact.claim: Nicknamed 'the Professor'. Rolling Stone's obituary headline called him the 'Rush Drummer Who Set a New Standard for Rock Virtuosity' (cited on Wikipedia).

signature_techniques.claim: Fast single-foot kick drumming: the 'Good Times Bad Times' bass-drum triplets, played on one pedal.
Hand-to-foot triplets that lead with the left hand (Dazed and Confused).
A variant of the Bernard Purdie half-time shuffle on 'Fool in the Rain'.
Bare hands on the drums during the 'Moby Dick' solo.
Later Zeppelin records include funk and Latin-influenced grooves.

gear.claim: Started on Premier. Carmine Appice introduced him to Ludwig in the late 1960s, and he used Ludwig for the rest of his career.
Typical Ludwig setup: 26x14 bass drum, 14x10 (later 15x12) rack tom, 16x16 and 18x16 floor toms.
On stage he used a Ludwig Supraphonic 402 snare (14x6.5) throughout his career.
The kit grew after 1969 to include congas or timpani and a gong.

feel.claim: Known for speed, power, a distinctive sound and a 'feel for groove' (AllMusic, as cited by Wikipedia).

influences.claim: Max Roach, Gene Krupa, Buddy Rich. Mostly self-taught.
In 1972 he named the Graham Bond Organisation (with Ginger Baker and Jack Bruce) as an influence from his school days.

arranging.claim: Said he used cymbals mainly 'to crash into a solo and out of it' and preferred 'the actual drum sound' (1973 interview, quoted in Mick Bonham's book, via fan site).

impact.claim: Regarded as one of the greatest and most influential drummers. Widely sampled in hip-hop: the Beastie Boys used Moby Dick, The Ocean and When the Levee Breaks, and Enigma's 'Return to Innocence' samples Levee.
His 'Fool in the Rain' shuffle is one strand of Jeff Porcaro's 'Rosanna' shuffle.

signature_techniques.claim: A left-handed player on a right-handed kit. He starts fills on the floor tom and moves up, and used open 'snatch' hi-hats to make room for fills (Rain).
Brought matched grip into the mainstream.
Played the Beatles' percussion parts too: maracas, tambourine, bongos, congas, timpani on 'Every Little Thing'.

gear.claim: Ludwig Black Oyster Pearl kit. The Ludwig logo on his bass drum made Ludwig the dominant North American drum maker for about 20 years.
Draped tea towels over the drums for a deep, muffled sound, for example on 'Come Together' and 'Something' (per Geoff Emerick).

feel.claim: Emphasised feel over technical virtuosity. Never plays over the vocal; 'Drummers hold it together.'

influences.claim: Named Cozy Cole's 'Topsy Part Two' as 'the one drum record' he bought, and said he 'was never really into drummers'.
Started in skiffle, then rock & roll with Rory Storm and the Hurricanes.

arranging.claim: Wrote song-specific drum parts that are identifiable without the rest of the music (Steve Smith). Saved fills for gaps in the vocal (Gregg Bissonette).

impact.claim: Influenced drummers to think compositionally, and spread matched grip, lower tuning and muffling. Inducted into the PAS Hall of Fame (2002) and Modern Drummer Hall of Fame (1999).

quotes.quote: Everyone put me down–said that I couldn't play. They didn't realize that was my style and I wasn't playing like anyone else–that I couldn't play like anyone else.

signature_techniques.claim: Reggae-inspired 'upside-down' grooves that don't just play a backbeat. He traces this to Desmond Dekker's 'Israelites'.
Uses the hi-hat as 'the upper level of the rhythm', with left-foot control of its texture. Plays off repeat-echo delay rhythms (Walking on the Moon).

gear.claim: Tama drums, Paiste cymbals, Remo heads, Vater sticks. Added Octobans. Helped Paiste design a splash cymbal. Relies heavily on 13-inch hi-hats.
In 1982: repeat echo on the hi-hat and Octobans, a Synare, and a dead Rototom under his left hand.

feel.claim: Says he aims for a 'full relaxed' Joe Morello-style sound, 'letting the drums sing'.

influences.claim: Buddy Rich (his drum hero at 14), Mitch Mitchell, Joe Morello, reggae drummers, and Arabic baladi rhythms from growing up in Beirut.
Grew up in Beirut listening to Lebanese music, rock and roll, jazz and reggae.

arranging.claim: Describes 'Every Breath You Take' as an outlier: a composed, overdubbed part with separate snare, hi-hat and kick takes.

impact.claim: Ranked the 10th-best drummer of all time by Rolling Stone. Peter Gabriel brought him in for 'Red Rain' and 'Big Time' for his 'hi-hat mastery'.

signature_techniques.claim: Plays with all four limbs carrying parts. He told Songlines 'the drums were made for four limbs', and Fela said he 'sounded like four drummers'.
Soft, subtle dynamics: 'flowing like a river'.

feel.claim: Relaxed and conversational. The drums 'ask a question' and the horns or guitar answer.

influences.claim: Jùjú, American jazz and highlife. Studied recordings by Art Blakey and Max Roach, as well as Ghanaian drummer Guy Warren (Kofi Ghanaba).

arranging.claim: Drummer and musical director of Fela Kuti's Africa '70 (1968–79) and a co-founder of Afrobeat.
Recorded with Hugh Masekela with nothing worked out in advance, building on his own 'drum patterns'.

impact.claim: Fela said 'without Tony Allen, there would be no Afrobeat'. Brian Eno called him 'perhaps the greatest drummer who has ever lived'. Collaborated with Damon Albarn (The Good, the Bad & the Queen; Rocket Juice & the Moon). Tributes on his death came from Flea, Peter Gabriel and others.

quotes.quote: Some drummers don't know what it means to play soft, it's not in their book

quotes.quote: I know I can make my drums bring the house down if I have to. But I know how to make it subtle. You listen to it flowing like a river.

quotes.quote: When I'm in a happy mood playing, you can hear me like six drummers. On some days it could be 100!

quotes.quote: But the drums were made for four limbs. A few jazz drummers use their four limbs, but most drummers don't. I want all my four limbs to be working.

quotes.quote: You don't ride a bicycle with one leg

quotes.quote: I like to have a conversation between the drums and other instruments. You ask a question with the drums and the guitar or saxophone answers.

signature_techniques.claim: Odd time signatures, polyrhythms and polymeters. Practises rudiments and snare solos with his feet.
Example meters: 'The Grudge' is mostly in five, 'Ticks and Leeches' is in 7/4 with tom accents in three over seven, and 'Lateralus' opens with 9/8, 8/8 and 7/4.
Tunes the toms to the song's key, for example a D-F-A triad for songs in D minor.
Studied tabla with Aloke Dutta, which you can hear on 'Disposition' and 'Right in Two'. He triggers tabla samples live from pads.

gear.claim: Sonor drums (including a 2009 signature 14x8 bronze snare), Paiste cymbals, Evans heads, Hammerax, and Mandala, Korg and Roland electronics.
Simmons SDX pads in 2001. Arranges his kit by golden-section ratios: five toms, six six-sided pads.

feel.claim: Wants a ritualistic, trance-like effect, sometimes emulating 'five African drummers' with polyrhythms.

influences.claim: Bill Bruford ('one of my biggest influences').
Billy Cobham and Buddy Rich for their articulation. Drum corps and rudimental training. Classical study in college.
Studied at the University of Missouri–Kansas City and played in the Kansas City jazz scene.

arranging.claim: Calls his role in Tool 'more like the music director' and takes part in a lot of the arranging.
Parts come out of long taped jams. He says there's 'never any mention of time signatures', and meters only come up when they're arranging.

quotes.quote: It's all about setting my drums up so that I don't get in the way of the music, so I'm just a channel for the music.

signature_techniques.claim: A session approach built on restraint: no cool fills in the first verse. He follows the bass and plans where the hi-hats open or close for each section.

gear.claim: Starts from a basic 'Ringo 4-piece' and adds per band. For A Perfect Circle: 2 racks, 2 floors, a second snare and more cymbals. For NIN: bigger drums (24 kick, 18 and 20 floors).

feel.claim: Says playing slow and making it feel right is the hard part, and that 'less is more' is a sign of maturity.

influences.claim: Jim Keltner, Steve Jordan, Jeff Porcaro, and songwriters. Grew up playing along to Van Halen, Queen and Devo.
Long relationships with Vinnie Colaiuta and Terry Bozzio since childhood.

arranging.claim: Asks how closely to follow the demo, opens up on choruses, and saves fills for the end or the solo.

impact.claim: Appears on 400+ albums since 1986. Member of The Vandals (since 1989), A Perfect Circle (1999–2012 and since 2024), Guns N' Roses (1997–99), and Foo Fighters (2023 until he was let go in May 2025).

quotes.quote: I learned the hard way about overplaying in the studio. At first I wanted to play everything I knew. But what's hard to do is to play slow and make that feel right.

quotes.quote: Learning about less is more is a sign of maturity.

quotes.quote: I got less into the circus tricks and more into people like Keltner, Jordan, and Porcaro.

signature_techniques.claim: Says he has always focused on his hands more than his feet; later System material pushed him to two bass drums instead of a double pedal.

gear.claim: In 2002: a Tama kit with five toms and a double pedal, timbales for a few songs, Paiste cymbals (around eleven), Remo heads and Bickford sticks.

influences.claim: Built his style playing along to records across genres. He names Keith Moon as his favorite drummer and Stewart Copeland as a huge influence.

arranging.claim: The band folds jazz, funk, metal, traditional Armenian, Middle Eastern and Latin music into its sound, which shapes his abrupt, stop-start parts.

impact.claim: Drummer of System of a Down since 1997, replacing Andy Khachaturian.

feel.claim: Self-taught; he says he never studied drums and does not read music.
Values consistency over perfect time; he plays to the room in the studio and says "Teen Spirit" sounded bigger because he played less.

influences.claim: Calls John Bonham "the greatest rock drummer of all time" and studied why Bonham played what he played.
Credits Dale Crover of the Melvins with showing him "there's a lot more to drumming", and still calls him the best drummer in the world.

impact.claim: Nirvana's drummer from 1990 (Nevermind, In Utero). He then founded Foo Fighters and drummed on Queens of the Stone Age's Songs for the Deaf and with Them Crooked Vultures.

signature_techniques.claim: The 'Rosanna shuffle': a half-time shuffle he said took its inspiration from Bernard Purdie ("Home at Last").
Built the groove of "Africa" from a one-bar tape loop of drums and percussion played with Lenny Castro, rather than a drum machine.
"Hold the Line" was him playing a Sly Stone, Greg Errico-style groove: triplets on the hi-hat under a hard rock backbeat.

gear.claim: In 1988: Pearl jazz-size toms (10, 12, 13, 14 and a 16 floor), an 18x22 bass drum, piccolo and metal snares, a Ludwig Black Beauty, and Paiste cymbals.

feel.claim: Credited his 16th-note feel to Paul Humphrey, Ed Greene, Earl Palmer and James Gadson, and his ballad playing to Jim Keltner, aiming to leave space.

impact.claim: Founding member of Toto and one of the most recorded session drummers of his era, including Steely Dan and Boz Scaggs. He died in 1992, aged 38.

signature_techniques.claim: Uses two bass drums mainly for speed on shuffles, and in the studio often works from a small kit: snare, kick, hi-hat, a cymbal and maybe one tom.

feel.claim: His aim is to be in the moment: rehearse, but leave room to make every night different.

influences.claim: Ginger Baker was his first model, a drummer who "made music on his drums". He also cites Bonham and Keith Moon, and prefers Louie Bellson to Buddy Rich.

impact.claim: Co-founded Van Halen with his brother Eddie and played on all of the band's studio albums.

signature_techniques.claim: A steady, unadorned backbeat played for the song; he rarely fills and never built a drum solo into the AC/DC show.

feel.claim: He hits hard, he says, because in the early days he had to be heard over walls of Marshalls, but "it's always about the groove and the feel".

influences.claim: Names Ringo Starr ("the greatest"), Simon Kirke and Ian Paice.

impact.claim: AC/DC's drummer from 1975 to 1983 and again from 1994, including Highway to Hell and Back in Black. Rammstein's Christoph Schneider called the band simple but "not so easy to copy".

signature_techniques.claim: Odd meters are central. He learned them by following piano and guitar songbooks of Rush and Yes records and counting the time signatures.

gear.claim: Famous for very large kits; his early-2000s touring "Siamese Monster" combined a big traditional kit with a smaller second setup.

influences.claim: His biggest progressive influence was Neil Peart, along with Bill Bruford and other prog drummers, after The Who, Led Zeppelin and The Beatles.

impact.claim: Co-founded Dream Theater at Berklee in 1985, left in 2010 and later rejoined.

quotes.quote: My biggest and most obvious progressive drumming influence was Neil Peart.

quotes.quote: I am a feel guy.

signature_techniques.claim: Large kits with two bass drums. The Mahavishnu Orchestra years pushed him to explore double bass after starting on a single kick.

feel.claim: Says the Mahavishnu Orchestra gave him complete freedom; as a leader he sets up a framework and leaves room to improvise.

influences.claim: Grew up in a family of drummers from Panama, hearing Latin and steel-drum music. He names Miles Davis, Tony Williams and Max Roach as landmarks.

impact.claim: Played on Miles Davis records and with the Mahavishnu Orchestra. His 1973 solo debut Spectrum (with "Stratus") is a jazz-rock touchstone.

quotes.quote: All I could do was just do what I do and hope that it worked, because there was no one to ask

signature_techniques.claim: Treated single strokes and the roll as the core of technique: fast singles close into a roll, and wrist control makes it sound like tearing sandpaper.

feel.claim: Self-taught; he says he never had a lesson. He felt a perfectly steady tempo was too mechanical to swing and preferred a band that pushes.

influences.claim: Called Chick Webb the greatest drummer who ever lived.

impact.claim: A child vaudeville star ("Traps the Drum Wonder") who played with Artie Shaw and Tommy Dorsey and later led his own big band.

quotes.quote: You must have the ability to control your wrist to a point where you can make your roll sound like you're tearing a piece of sandpaper.

signature_techniques.claim: His tom-tom interludes on Benny Goodman's "Sing, Sing, Sing" were the first extended drum solos recorded commercially.

impact.claim: He raised the drummer from accompanist to solo voice. In 1978 he became the first drummer inducted into the Modern Drummer Hall of Fame.
Joined Goodman in December 1934 and left after the January 1938 Carnegie Hall concert to lead his own orchestra.

quotes.quote: I made the drummer a high-priced guy, and I was able to project enough so that I was able to draw more people to jazz.
quotes.source_title: Gene Krupa – Not Bad for a Young Upstart

feel.claim: Studied jazz from a young age and played in his high school jazz ensemble and marching band. He rejects the "punk drummer" label.

arranging.claim: On the untitled 2003 blink-182 album many songs began from his drum ideas; he also tracked songs with both big and small kits.

impact.claim: Joined blink-182 in 1998 (first full album: Enema of the State) and has worked widely in hip-hop and pop as well.

quotes.quote: I love punk rock drumming, but there is so much more stuff out there that can influence your playing, like playing shuffles.

quotes.quote: One thing inspires the other, and that's what's great about learning different styles.

quotes.quote: And a lot of ideas came from the drum parts.

influences.claim: Started with Ian Paice, then emulated Mitch Mitchell, Bill Ward and John Bonham for their "jazzy swing". Later Stewart Copeland and Neil Peart.

arranging.claim: Trusts first instincts: about 80% of the time his first idea becomes the part. He shapes his parts around Anthony Kiedis's rhythmic vocals.

impact.claim: Red Hot Chili Peppers drummer since 1988; also Chickenfoot.

quotes.quote: Eighty percent of the time, the first thing I come up with ends up being the thing, which is pretty cool, because it's pure

quotes.quote: The way Anthony sings is very rhythmic.

quotes.quote: I tried to emulate Mitch and Bill Ward and John Bonham because they all had that jazzy swing.

signature_techniques.claim: The "50 Ways to Leave Your Lover" intro grew out of drum-corps-style patterns he was practicing between takes: hi-hat, snare and bass drum, hi-hat with the left hand.

influences.claim: Grew up on Krupa, Buddy Rich, Max Roach, Elvin Jones, Philly Joe Jones, Tony Williams and Art Blakey. Then New York funk players turned him toward the groove.

arranging.claim: The "Aja" drums were cut live with the band, and Wayne Shorter overdubbed his solo afterwards.

impact.claim: One of the most recorded drummers in pop and jazz, with Paul Simon, Steely Dan, Eric Clapton, Chick Corea and James Taylor.

quotes.quote: I was practicing between takes. That's how that started.
quotes.source_title: Steve Gadd on Aja, 50 Ways to Leave Your Lover...: Gimme Five

quotes.quote: When you do a session like that, you do whatever makes it work for the artist, and you hope it will be a hit - but you never know.
quotes.source_title: Steve Gadd on Aja, 50 Ways to Leave Your Lover...: Gimme Five

quotes.quote: We did the song live in the studio and then Wayne overdubbed his parts after.
quotes.source_title: Steve Gadd on Aja, 50 Ways to Leave Your Lover...: Gimme Five

quotes.quote: Then I got to New York and started hearing some funk players, so I started to concentrate more on the groove than on the freedom of straight-ahead stuff.
quotes.source_title: Steve Gadd: Opens Up

signature_techniques.claim: Studied privately with Alan Dawson, and practiced hands on a pad for hours a day; he considered his hands the most important thing.

feel.claim: In his words, the drummer's first job is time, then bridging the other instruments and making them comfortable.

influences.claim: Named Max Roach, Philly Joe Jones, Art Blakey, Jo Jones, Sid Catlett and Kenny Clarke.

impact.claim: Joined Miles Davis's quintet at 17 and later led the fusion band Lifetime. He died in 1997.
